events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and true blast radius for notification-service. Determine: (1) exact first onset of abnormal memory growth / OOMKilled events this week (all three restarts) and whether they predate today's Kafka maintenance; (2) whether consumer lag spikes lead or lag the restarts (cause vs consequence); (3) memory trend (RSS/heap) shape — steady leak vs step increase vs throughput-correlated; (4) whether any OTHER services show simultaneous resource/error anomalies (shared component signal). Query logs and metrics for notification-service and neighboring services around 2026-03-23T20:00Z and across the week.

Find what changed and when across ALL services in the week before the incident and specifically around today's Kafka maintenance. List: deployments (esp. notification-service and anything it depends on), config changes (Kafka topic/retention/consumer-group settings, memory limits/requests, HPA), dependency graph of notification-service (upstream Kafka, downstream email provider, shared libs/services), and any historical precedent incidents involving OOMKilled + consumer lag or Kafka replay. Return timestamps for each change.

Validate or refute the Kafka-replay theory specifically: quantify whether a replay/backlog burst actually reached notification-service (consumer group lag volume, message rate, partition skew) after the maintenance window, and whether memory consumption correlates with message volume or with message content/size. Also check whether the OOM is triggered by processing a specific message type (e.g. large trade-confirmation batch) or by retry/buffer accumulation. Conclude with the strongest evidence-based cause hypothesis given the onset and blast-radius data.

args.query: OOMKilled consumer lag Kafka replay memory

events.statement: Across ALL services, only two deployments occurred in the week before the incident: notification-service v3.8.0 at 2026-03-21T00:00:00Z ('Add in-memory template cache for email rendering', status live, not rolled back) and auth-service v7.1.4 at 2026-03-22T13:00:00Z (patch, bump jackson). No notification-service deployment after 2026-03-21.

The only config change anywhere in the window was on kafka: log.retention.ms reduced from 604800000 (7 days) to 259200000 (3 days) at 2026-03-23T18:00:00Z by platform-team, described as 'Kafka maintenance: reduce retention to 3 days'. This is the 'today's Kafka maintenance' referenced in the report and is ~2h20m before the 20:20Z report.

A dedicated query for config changes across all services in 2026-03-19 to 2026-03-21 returned count 0, so there were no config/flag changes (e.g. HPA, memory limits, consumer-group or topic settings) registered in the days immediately preceding the deployment.

Dependency graph of notification-service: it has edges to kafka (kind 'queue-consume') and to email-provider (kind 'external', vendor-owned, has_telemetry=false). kafka is marked shared=true (owner platform); notification-service itself is has_telemetry=true, shared=false. No upstream edges into notification-service were returned (empty edge set), so no producing service is registered as a caller.

Two historical precedent incidents match the symptom pattern: HIST-104 (2025-11-05, notification-service + kafka, consumer lag spike/delayed emails, root cause 'Partition reassignment caused consumer group rebalancing storm') and HIST-112 (2026-02-03, settlement-service + kafka, consumer lag growing, root cause 'Consumer lost partition assignment during broker maintenance'). Neither precedes today's reported OOMKilled restarts directly, and the search notes past incidents are leads, not evidence about the current incident.

No deployment or config change is recorded on or after the 2026-03-23 18:00Z Kafka maintenance, nor between the 2026-03-21 template-cache deploy and the maintenance — the change surface between the last code change (2026-03-21) and the incident is only the kafka retention reduction.

events.description: No memory-limit/request or HPA config change for notification-service was found, and get_config_changes(kafka) returned only log.retention.ms. There is no data confirming or denying a change to notification-service memory limits, consumer-group settings (e.g. max.poll.records, fetch sizes) or replica/HPA settings in the window; config-change scope may only cover a limited set of keys.
get_service_dependencies(notification-service, direction=upstream) and (kafka, downstream) both returned empty edge sets.

get_deployments and get_config_changes appear to cover only service-level entries; no Kafka broker-level software upgrade record for 'today's Kafka maintenance' beyond the log.retention.ms config change was returned.

events.answer: Only two deployments in the week before the incident (notification-service v3.8.0 on 2026-03-21 adding an in-memory template cache, and auth-service v7.1.4 on 2026-03-22) and exactly one config change in the whole window: a Kafka log.retention.ms reduction from 7 days to 3 days at 2026-03-23T18:00:00Z. notification-service consumes from the shared `kafka` cluster and calls the external `email-provider`; no upstream callers were returned. Two past incidents (HIST-104, HIST-112) match the symptom pattern of consumer lag + delayed notifications after Kafka broker/partition maintenance.

events.statement: notification-service OOMKilled (exit code 137) occurred exactly three times this week, at 2026-03-21T22:59:50Z, 2026-03-22T21:59:47Z and 2026-03-23T19:59:21Z — all three predate/are unrelated to a single maintenance event, and the 03-23 restart happened BEFORE the 20:20Z report.

The cumulative restarts metric steps 0→1 in the 2026-03-21T22:00 bucket, 1→2 in the 2026-03-22T22:00 bucket, and 2→3 in the 2026-03-23T20:00 bucket (bucket_seconds=7200), matching three distinct restart events.

Memory (memory_pct) is a slow steady climb, not a step: on 03-23 it rose from ~46% at 20:00 (post-restart) to 55.48% by 23:50, a gain of ~1 point per ~10 min, and pre-restart it sat pinned near 96-98% (max 98.44 at 19:40). Post-restart the container resumes climbing immediately.

Consumer lag spikes occur in the SAME/first bucket as the restart and are ~50-70 messages immediately before, then jump to 18137.93 at 19:55Z and decay afterwards (14213 at 20:00, 10374 at 20:05, 3600 at 20:15, back to 50.65 at 20:25) — i.e. the lag spike coincides with/after the OOM, not before it; lag is a consequence of the restart, not a leading cause.

Request throughput was flat and normal across the onset (~118-142 req/s throughout 18:30-21:30Z, including the 19:55 spike window), so the memory climb is NOT throughput-correlated — the OOM is not driven by a traffic/load surge.

The week-22 lag spikes are not unique to 03-23: consumer_lag also spiked in the 2026-03-21T22:00 bucket (avg 2273.11, max 17161.92) and 2026-03-22T20:00/22:00 buckets (avg 790.21/1589.77, max 17611.66/14375.74), each aligned with an OOM restart, showing the same restart→lag pattern repeats.

events.answer: notification-service suffered three OOMKilled restarts this week at 2026-03-21T22:59:50Z, 2026-03-22T21:59:47Z and 2026-03-23T19:59:21Z. Memory is a slow steady climb (pinned ~96-98% before the 03-23 crash, resuming immediately after restart), NOT throughput-correlated (request_rate flat ~118-142 req/s throughout). Consumer lag spikes coincide with/decay after each restart (18137.93 at 19:55Z then decaying to 50.65 by 20:25Z), so lag is a consequence of the restart, not a leading cause — the replay/maintenance hypothesis is not supported by lag leading the OOM. No other service was confirmed anomalous (order-service logs empty), and broker-side telemetry was not queried.

events.statement: notification-service consumer_lag was NORMAL (well under 100 messages) throughout 18:00-19:40Z and only spiked to 18137.93 max in the 19:50Z bucket, the same bucket as the 19:59:21Z OOMKilled restart; it then decayed (14213.61 max at 20:00, 7499.81 at 20:10, 286.99 at 20:20, 71.58 at 20:30). No lag buildup precedes the crash.

Message/request throughput did NOT surge around the onset: request_rate stayed flat 117.85-142.43 req/s across 18:00-21:00Z (141.2 avg / 141.93 max in the 19:50 bucket itself), and latency_p99_ms stayed flat 101.97-117.13 ms. So neither a traffic burst nor a processing-rate change is present.

An in-memory template cache grows monotonically and has never evicted an entry: TemplateCache stats show size=51750 entries, evictions=0 (03-21T05:45:44Z) → 103500 entries, evictions=0 (03-21T11:30:16Z) → 155250 entries, evictions=0 (03-21T17:15:45Z) → 196650 entries, evictions=0 (03-21T21:51:13Z) → 188100 entries, evictions=0 (03-23T18:54:31Z). This is unbounded, content-driven accumulation, not message-volume-driven.

The memory pressure is old-generation heap exhaustion, not a throughput/heap-transient pattern: repeated 'heap usage N% over 90 (old gen)' full-GC warnings with escalating pause times (4152ms → 5072ms → 6388ms → 6488ms) in the hours before the 19:59:21Z OOMKilled restart. The heap warnings first appear 2026-03-21T21:37:01Z, hours after the v3.8.0 template-cache deployment (03-21T00:00:14Z) and before any Kafka maintenance.

memory_pct confirms content/leak-style growth independent of the restart: 93.73% at 18:00Z climbing to 96.78% (max 98.44) by 19:50Z, then a drop to 46.45% at 20:00Z immediately after the 19:59:21Z OOMKilled restart, after which it resumes climbing (47.87% at 21:00Z) at a steady ~1 point/10 min.

The same restart→lag pattern (lag spike only coincident with the crash, no pre-crash buildup) is consistent with T1's finding that all three OOMKilled restarts predate the single 2026-03-23T18:00Z Kafka retention change, so the maintenance cannot be the trigger for the earlier two crashes.

The 03-21/03-22 log window query returned truncated=true (40 of 151 matched), so full heap-GC and TemplateCache history for those two earlier crashes was not fully enumerated.

events.answer: The Kafka-replay theory is refuted. There is no evidence of a replay/backlog burst reaching notification-service: consumer_lag sat at a normal ~31-93 messages for the entire 18:00-19:40Z window before the OOM and only jumped to 18137.93 at 19:50Z — in the same bucket as the 19:59:21Z OOMKilled restart — then decayed back to normal. That lag is a consequence of the consumer dying, not a cause. Message throughput (request_rate 117-142 req/s) and p99 latency (~110ms) were flat and normal across the onset, so memory is not throughput/message-volume correlated. Instead, the one deployment in the window (notification-service v3.8.0, 03-21, "Add in-memory template cache") introduced an unbounded cache that grows monotonically (51,750 → 103,500 → 155,250 → 188,100 → 196,650 entries, evictions=0) and drives old-gen heap exhaustion with escalating full-GC times. The strongest evidence-based hypothesis is an unbounded in-memory template cache (content-cache accumulation, not Kafka replay) as the memory-growth driver.

events.title: Unbounded in-memory template cache introduced by notification-service v3.8.0 causes old-gen heap exhaustion and OOMKilled restarts
Kafka retention reduction to 3 days triggered a replay that notification-service choked on
Shared dependency (email-provider, Kafka broker, or template/rendering service) degradation causes notification-service to buffer retries in memory
Memory is a pre-existing resource-exhaustion / unrecorded limit change rather than a new fault

events.summary: H1 (unbounded in-memory template cache from v3.8.0) is well grounded and beats all alternatives. Grounding: every hop rests on verified findings — F1 (v3.8.0 03-21T00:00Z, 'Add in-memory template cache', only notification-service deploy), F15 (cache size 51750→196650, evictions=0, monotonic, content-driven not volume-driven), F16 (old-gen heap warnings with escalating full-GC pauses, first at 03-21T21:37Z, hours after deploy and before any Kafka change), F7/F8 (exactly three OOMKilled exit-137 restarts 03-21/03-22/03-23), F9/F17 (slow steady memory_pct climb, pinned 96-98% pre-crash, resumes immediately post-restart, ~1pt/10min). Temporal order: cause (03-21T00:00Z deploy) precedes onset (03-21T21:37Z heap warning, 22:59Z first OOM) by ~22h, and the ~24h cadence is consistent. Scope: OOMs are confined to notification-service, which is has_telemetry=true and not shared; no other service was confirmed anomalous. Alternatives were genuinely tested, not dismissed: H2 refuted by timing (two of three restarts precede the 18:00Z retention change) AND mechanism (lag normal <100 through 19:40Z, spiking only in the same bucket as the 19:59Z crash, decaying after — F10/F13), plus flat throughput/latency (F11/F14) negating a replay burst. H3's two causal hops are explicitly unevidenced and contradicted by the same flat-lag/flat-throughput data and by content-driven cache growth. H4 is contradicted by F15/F16 (growth is new and tied to a specific deploy) and no config/limit change was found (F3/F6). Remaining weaknesses are bounded: no pre-03-21 baseline, no RSS/heap split, and a config-coverage gap that could hide an unrecorded limit change. These support a confidence_cap near 0.75-0.78 rather than blocking, since cache disable/plateau is a recovery action and a limit change alone cannot explain an evictionless monotonic cache introduced this week.

events.why: top hypothesis is above threshold and clearly ahead

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and true blast radius for notification-service. Determine: (1) exact first onset of abnormal memory growth / OOMKilled events this week (all three restarts) and whether they predate today's Kafka maintenance; (2) whether consumer lag spikes lead or lag the restarts (cause vs consequence); (3) memory trend (RSS/heap) shape — steady leak vs step increase vs throughput-correlated; (4) whether any OTHER services show simultaneous resource/error anomalies (shared component signal). Query logs and metrics for notification-service and neighboring services around 2026-03-23T20:00Z and across the week.
tasks.answer: notification-service suffered three OOMKilled restarts this week at 2026-03-21T22:59:50Z, 2026-03-22T21:59:47Z and 2026-03-23T19:59:21Z. Memory is a slow steady climb (pinned ~96-98% before the 03-23 crash, resuming immediately after restart), NOT throughput-correlated (request_rate flat ~118-142 req/s throughout). Consumer lag spikes coincide with/decay after each restart (18137.93 at 19:55Z then decaying to 50.65 by 20:25Z), so lag is a consequence of the restart, not a leading cause — the replay/maintenance hypothesis is not supported by lag leading the OOM. No other service was confirmed anomalous (order-service logs empty), and broker-side telemetry was not queried.

tasks.objective: Find what changed and when across ALL services in the week before the incident and specifically around today's Kafka maintenance. List: deployments (esp. notification-service and anything it depends on), config changes (Kafka topic/retention/consumer-group settings, memory limits/requests, HPA), dependency graph of notification-service (upstream Kafka, downstream email provider, shared libs/services), and any historical precedent incidents involving OOMKilled + consumer lag or Kafka replay. Return timestamps for each change.
tasks.answer: Only two deployments in the week before the incident (notification-service v3.8.0 on 2026-03-21 adding an in-memory template cache, and auth-service v7.1.4 on 2026-03-22) and exactly one config change in the whole window: a Kafka log.retention.ms reduction from 7 days to 3 days at 2026-03-23T18:00:00Z. notification-service consumes from the shared `kafka` cluster and calls the external `email-provider`; no upstream callers were returned. Two past incidents (HIST-104, HIST-112) match the symptom pattern of consumer lag + delayed notifications after Kafka broker/partition maintenance.

tasks.objective: Validate or refute the Kafka-replay theory specifically: quantify whether a replay/backlog burst actually reached notification-service (consumer group lag volume, message rate, partition skew) after the maintenance window, and whether memory consumption correlates with message volume or with message content/size. Also check whether the OOM is triggered by processing a specific message type (e.g. large trade-confirmation batch) or by retry/buffer accumulation. Conclude with the strongest evidence-based cause hypothesis given the onset and blast-radius data.
tasks.answer: The Kafka-replay theory is refuted. There is no evidence of a replay/backlog burst reaching notification-service: consumer_lag sat at a normal ~31-93 messages for the entire 18:00-19:40Z window before the OOM and only jumped to 18137.93 at 19:50Z — in the same bucket as the 19:59:21Z OOMKilled restart — then decayed back to normal. That lag is a consequence of the consumer dying, not a cause. Message throughput (request_rate 117-142 req/s) and p99 latency (~110ms) were flat and normal across the onset, so memory is not throughput/message-volume correlated. Instead, the one deployment in the window (notification-service v3.8.0, 03-21, "Add in-memory template cache") introduced an unbounded cache that grows monotonically (51,750 → 103,500 → 155,250 → 188,100 → 196,650 entries, evictions=0) and drives old-gen heap exhaustion with escalating full-GC times. The strongest evidence-based hypothesis is an unbounded in-memory template cache (content-cache accumulation, not Kafka replay) as the memory-growth driver.

critiques.summary: H1 (unbounded in-memory template cache from v3.8.0) is well grounded and beats all alternatives. Grounding: every hop rests on verified findings — F1 (v3.8.0 03-21T00:00Z, 'Add in-memory template cache', only notification-service deploy), F15 (cache size 51750→196650, evictions=0, monotonic, content-driven not volume-driven), F16 (old-gen heap warnings with escalating full-GC pauses, first at 03-21T21:37Z, hours after deploy and before any Kafka change), F7/F8 (exactly three OOMKilled exit-137 restarts 03-21/03-22/03-23), F9/F17 (slow steady memory_pct climb, pinned 96-98% pre-crash, resumes immediately post-restart, ~1pt/10min). Temporal order: cause (03-21T00:00Z deploy) precedes onset (03-21T21:37Z heap warning, 22:59Z first OOM) by ~22h, and the ~24h cadence is consistent. Scope: OOMs are confined to notification-service, which is has_telemetry=true and not shared; no other service was confirmed anomalous. Alternatives were genuinely tested, not dismissed: H2 refuted by timing (two of three restarts precede the 18:00Z retention change) AND mechanism (lag normal <100 through 19:40Z, spiking only in the same bucket as the 19:59Z crash, decaying after — F10/F13), plus flat throughput/latency (F11/F14) negating a replay burst. H3's two causal hops are explicitly unevidenced and contradicted by the same flat-lag/flat-throughput data and by content-driven cache growth. H4 is contradicted by F15/F16 (growth is new and tied to a specific deploy) and no config/limit change was found (F3/F6). Remaining weaknesses are bounded: no pre-03-21 baseline, no RSS/heap split, and a config-coverage gap that could hide an unrecorded limit change. These support a confidence_cap near 0.75-0.78 rather than blocking, since cache disable/plateau is a recovery action and a limit change alone cannot explain an evictionless monotonic cache introduced this week.

challenges.issue: No pre-2026-03-20 memory baseline (restarts series only from 03-20T00:00Z). The claim that the climb is NEW and began with the 03-21 deploy is inferred from the deploy+heap-warning coincidence, not from a flat pre-deploy baseline.

Cache contribution to the ~50% memory baseline is unproven: only memory_pct exists, no RSS/heap split, so the ~196650-entry cache's byte cost vs total RSS is not quantified. Assumption flagged by the reasoner but not closed.
Config-change coverage may be incomplete (F3/F6 cover only a limited key set); an unrecorded notification-service memory limit/HPA change was not positively ruled out.

Two causal hops are unevidenced and the hypothesis rests on the email-provider being unobservable (has_telemetry=false); however, flat throughput/latency (F11/F14) and content-driven (not volume-driven) cache growth (F15) argue against retry-buffer accumulation, so it is not a live competitor.

Not fully excluded only because of the config-coverage gap; but F15/F16 (new evictionless cache + first heap warning hours after the deploy, before any other change) leave it as a weak fallback rather than a plausible co-equal origin.

Broker-side telemetry (partition reassignment/replay volume around 18:00Z) was never queried, so the replay mechanism is refuted only from the consumer side (lag/throughput). Consumer-side evidence is sufficient for ranking because no lag buildup precedes any crash, and two of three crashes predate the change.
